reason: The pointwise limit is identified, and the negation of uniform convergence is verified with a fixed positive epsilon.
text:
For each \(x\in[0,1)\), \(x^n\to 0\), while \(f_n(1)=1\) for every \(n\). Hence the pointwise limit is
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x=1.\end{cases}
\]
If \((f_n)\) converged uniformly, its uniform limit would necessarily be \(f\). Set \(\varepsilon=\tfrac12\). For every \(N\in\mathbb Z_+\), choose \(n=N\) and \(x=2^{-1/N}\in[0,1)\). Then \(f(x)=0\) and
\[
|f_n(x)-f(x)|=x^N=\frac12.
\]
Thus, for every \(N\), there exist \(n\ge N\) and \(x\in[0,1]\) such that \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|\ge\varepsilon\), contradicting the definition of uniform convergence. Therefore \((f_n)\) does not converge uniformly on \([0,1]\).
